bibliography.checked_against: the article's first page and running heads (Journal of Ecology 2006, 94, 558–568) and Crossref
bibliography.note: Anna E. Marburg, Monica G. Turner & Timothy K. Kratz; issue 3 is from Crossref (not printed on the pages)

claims.claim: 45 Vilas County, WI lakes; pieces ≥ 150 cm long crossing the 0.5-m contour
claims.quote: crossed the transect and at least 150 cm in length
claims.conditions: every piece ≥ 5 cm in diameter where it crossed a 50-m transect along the half-metre depth contour, and ≥ 150 cm long (line-intersect); eight sites per lake; 45 lakes in Vilas County, Wisconsin (35 chosen across the 1996 building-density range, plus low-development lakes)
MEDIAN (minimum–maximum) across the 12 lakes; each lake's value the mean of eight sites; pieces per km of the 0.5-m contour
claims.note: Read on the page image: the values are right. The table should say 'median' in this column too (it does only for the 45-lake column), and the asterisk ('read from a misaligned table extraction; corroborated by Weis & Sass') can go

claims.conditions: median (minimum–maximum) across 45 lakes spanning the development gradient

claims.claim: lakes with more than 9 buildings/km never had more than 200 pieces (logs) per km
claims.location: p. 562 (PDF p. 5), Results; restated p. 564 (PDF p. 7), Discussion
claims.quote: lakes with > 9 buildings km−1 never had more than 200 pieces
claims.conditions: 'buildings' = all buildings within 100 m of the lake per km of shoreline, from 1996 county data (p. 560: 'computed the number of buildings within 100 m of each lake'); wood ≥ 5 cm (Fig. 2a) and ≥ 10 cm (Fig. 2b) both declined with building density
claims.note: §3.2.9 compares this with Hot Brook's ~2 dwellings/km counted within ~200 m of the water: Marburg's metric counts every building within 100 m, so the two densities are not the same measure (the comparison still holds by a wide margin)

claims.claim: even under one method, undeveloped lakes differed by up to 13-fold
claims.quote: why undeveloped lakes have up to a 13-fold difference in coarse wood abundance
claims.conditions: the 12 low-development lakes: 27.5–375 pieces/km ≥ 5 cm (13.6-fold); for wood ≥ 10 cm, 15–280 (18.7-fold; reader's arithmetic from Table 1b)
214 of the 352 sites with complete data, 45 lakes
the 214 sites where wood was present

claims.claim: its best predictor was downed wood on the forest floor beside the lake (partial R² 0.48–0.54), not live-tree density
claims.location: p. 563 (PDF p. 6) and p. 564 (PDF p. 7), Results; Summary point 5, p. 558
claims.quote: density of riparian coarse wood (partial R2 = 0.54, P < 0.01)
claims.conditions: 'riparian coarse wood' = logs (dead trees touching the ground at two or more points, ≥ 10 cm) per ha in riparian plots; partial R² 0.54 among all 45 lakes, 0.48 among the 12 low-development lakes; neither tree density nor stand basal area correlated with littoral wood

claims.quote: proportion of the lake surrounded by wetlands (partial R2 = 0.21
claims.conditions: a LAKE-level effect in the 12 low-development lakes (share of the shoreline in wetlands, negative); at the site level wetland presence entered only one of 22 candidate models
claims.note: say 'lakes with more wetland shoreline held less' rather than implying a site-level effect

claims.quote: All of the final models included the relative exposure to wave action
claims.conditions: site level, the 214 sites with wood: every one of the 22 best models had a negative term for relative exposure (fetch-weighted wave height)

notes: Every value checks. Two presentation fixes for Table 3.2-5: label the low-development values as medians, and drop the asterisk about a misaligned extraction (the page image confirms the numbers). Other useful values: Table 1 gives riparian forest structure (e.g. riparian coarse wood median 225 logs/ha, 25–579, in all lakes; 431, 115–579, in low-development lakes); the lowest-AIC within-lake model was (−) exposure + riparian CW + beaver-chewed littoral CW; the maximum in undeveloped lakes was ~200 logs/km below earlier reports from very small (< 25 ha) protected lakes (p. 564–565).
